fields.sample_size: 489 housing units sampled (10% of the primary sampling units: 20% of each of 49 residential suburbs, stratified into 32 high-, 3 medium- and 14 low-density suburbs of 29,973 housing units); 411 questionnaires returned (84%); purposively sampled key informants from the city council (e.g. Director of Housing) and the Gweru Ratepayers and Residents Association; observation
fields.effect_measure: descriptive percentages and mean monthly water bills by suburb density (Table 3); ANOVA of incomes across suburbs (p = 0.231); household food security judged against the ZimStat Total Consumption Poverty Line (US$95.93 per person, about US$480 for a family of five); SPSS 20
fields.effect_estimate: Of 411 respondents, 97% had incomes below the food poverty datum line (only 3% earned above US$500 a month; average household income about US$55) and incomes did not differ across suburbs (ANOVA p = 0.231). Own food production (61%) and purchasing (84%) were the main food sources (45% used both). Average monthly water bills were US$29 in high-density, US$33 in medium-density and US$58 in low-density suburbs; 70% said bills were too high for their incomes. The municipality, with unreliable central-government grants and after the 2013 debt cancellation, prioritised revenue collection and intensified water cuts; central government has not subsidised water services for years. The authors conclude that water governance failures crippled household food security and recommend using wastewater and non-potable water for food gardens.

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a mixed-methods household survey (489 housing units sampled, 411 returned) and key-informant study of water governance and household food security in Gweru, Zimbabwe; read in full text 2026-10-04. Descriptive percentages and mean bills; one ANOVA.
